spike_candidates.statement: In 1965-66 Fred Trump bought Steeplechase Park, never reopened it, held a brick-throwing demolition party and bulldozed it before it could be landmarked.
spike_candidates.tension: The loss of one park created a worldwide impression that all of Coney Island had closed, and Trump never built the housing he wanted.

spike_candidates.statement: After Hurricane Sandy the beach lost about 600,000 cubic yards of sand, but the flooding that hurt people most came from Coney Island Creek, not the ocean.
spike_candidates.tension: Rebuilt sand dunes saved an estimated $494 million, yet the creek that flooded homes is toxic and still has no cleanup plan.

spike_candidates.statement: A draft $52 billion Army Corps plan would raise the boardwalk five feet with a concrete barrier covering about a third of it, with construction starting around 2030.
spike_candidates.tension: Protecting the beach from storms could wall off ocean views and change the boardwalk the city fought over in 2012.

spike_candidates.statement: In 2012 the city's design commission voted 6-0 to replace part of the 1923 wooden boardwalk with concrete and recycled plastic lumber.
spike_candidates.tension: Residents who said it would turn a boardwalk into a sidewalk lost in the review process and, per CBS 2014, in court.

conflicts: Sand volumes: Marine Technology says 600,000 cubic yards LOST in Sandy (P046) and about 580,000 cubic yards PLACED in 2013 (P047). The scout's '580k vs 600k' contradiction is two different measures, not a rounding disagreement. The 2013 Dredging Today page body is empty so the $7.2M / 600,000 figure could not be checked. Marine Technology (agency quote) is better than a blog but is still press.

Sea Gate sand: Dredging Today 2015 plans about 125,000 cubic yards (P053); Marine Technology 2023 says 75,000 cubic yards were placed in 2016 (P054); scout notes cite about 70,000 and 35,000 which are not in the bundle. Planned vs placed; prefer the 2023 Army Corps-quoted figure for what was placed, and say work was still underway in January 2015.

Aquarium dates: 6sqft says Moses moved the aquarium to the Dreamland site in 1947 (P003); WNYC says cornerstone 1954 (P021), first stage done 1956, re-opened 1957 (P022). WNYC (with archive citations) is more authoritative. 1947 is likely a plan or land assignment, not an opening.

Trump purchase date: 6sqft says February 1965 (P007); Untapped says 1964 (P008). Neither is a primary record; Steeplechase operated through 1964 per CHPC (P006), so 1965 is more plausible. Demolition: 6sqft says 1966 (P010); Untapped gives no year.

Moses rezoning: CHPC says April 2, 1953 proposal (P004) with housing from 1954 (P005); 6sqft says Moses built high-rises 'in the late 50s' and CN says the Coney Island Houses opened 1956 (P025). Use CHPC for the proposal and say projects arrived through the 1950s-60s.

Horseshoe crab age: Parks horseshoe-crab page says more than 300 million years (P078 source); the Parks Coney Island Creek Natural Area page says roughly 1.2 billion years. Both are NYC Parks; use 300 million (or avoid), and note the 1.2 billion figure is out of line with the species record.

Horseshoe crab sites: highlights page says crabs come ashore on Coney Island Beach (P077); the Parks crab page's Brooklyn list names Plumb Beach, Gerritsen Beach, Kaiser Park and Calvert Vaux Park but not Coney Island Beach (P081). The scout's 'monitoring since 2013' is not in the bundle; the Calvert Vaux page says the habitat beach was designed in 2011 (P082).

Boardwalk costs: 2011 article says concrete $90 vs $114 for concrete+plastic (P072); 2012 article says $90 is about $40 cheaper than real wood (P067), which implies wood at about $130, a different baseline. Carriage lane width: 12 feet (P065, 2011-12) vs 10 feet (CBS 2014); project cost $30 million for the 2.7 miles (2010) vs $10 million for the 2014 phase. These are different phases and years; do not blend them.

Brooklyn Paper 2012 calls the boardwalk '79-year-old' while the same article says it opened in 1923 (which would be 89 in 2012). Use 1923 (P066, P087; also Marine Technology's 100th birthday in 2023, P050).

HATS comment deadline: first CIHP post (Sept 2022) says Jan 6, 2023; second post (Feb 2023) says March 31, 2023 (P062). The later date reflects an extension; prefer the later post. Construction in 2030 (P061) is from the 2022 draft and may be stale.

Sea-level rate: THE CITY says NYC sea level rises faster than the global average (P101); City Limits (an activist's claim) says nearly double the global average. Prefer THE CITY (cites NPCC). Older NPCC range 0.5-2.5 ft by 2050s vs newest 1-2 ft; the scout's older '11-21 in' is not in the bundle.

Creek contaminants: scout said PAHs and cyanide; the bundle documents lead, mercury, pesticides (P093), PCBs, lead, benzene (CL), cyanide and mirex (P097). PAHs do not appear in any bundle source. Superfund: no source here says the creek was added to the NPL; the Nov 2023 status is under state review (P098).

Sandy cause: myth that ocean waves destroyed Coney: Hammerman says creek flooding hurt most (P056, single activist quote, medium), while Marine Technology says the surge pushed sand and water over the boardwalk (P049). Both are true in different places; the bundle has no official Parks damage report.

Scout-flagged items: Astroland 1962 open and Sept 7, 2008 close CONFIRMED (P028, P037); Luna Park May 29, 2010 CONFIRMED (P038); Council vote July 29, 2009 CONFIRMED but 44-2 and Thor $95.6M NOT in bundle (P041); Steeplechase 'last day Sept 20, 1964' and 'Sept 21, 1966 party' NOT in bundle; rumor that Trump rushed to beat landmarking is source-reported (P011) and unproven; FEMA $1.2M boardwalk-lights figure NOT in bundle.
dead_ends: Beach length and width in feet or miles (only the boardwalk, 2.7 miles per Brooklyn Paper 2012).
1994-95 renourishment and Coney Island shoreline project history 1995-2004 beyond the chief's name in Marine Technology.
West End and Sea Gate groin history before 2013.
Current boardwalk surface and which sections are wood, concrete or plastic (all sources 2011-2015).
2025-26 status of the Army Corps HATS plan, tide gate and five-foot boardwalk raise.
Any 2024-2026 EPA or NPL decision on Coney Island Creek.
Seals, piping plovers or other wildlife actually seen on Coney Island Beach.
1970s-80s arson, crime statistics, and public-housing tower specifics (only passing mentions).
Official Parks damage report for Sandy; Sandy water depths on the boardwalk.
Date and vote count of the 2009 Council vote (44-2), Thor Equities $95.6M city deal, and City Planning documents; only the July 29 date is in the bundle.
NPCC primary report (only a news summary is available); water quality testing data for the ocean beach itself.

recency.newest_item: Wikipedia Astroland page last edited 5 Oct 2026 and NYC Parks pages (2026) naming council members Kayla Santosuosso and Inna Vernikov; newest news in bundle is THE CITY Jan 2024 and City Limits Nov 2023. The Coney Island History Project site (2026) lists an April 16 Coney Island Creek resilience project event and exhibit season extended through October 11.

facts.fact: Luna Park burned in 1944 and closed in 1946, which thinned Coney Island's amusements and drew developer interest.
facts.quote: competitor luna park also caught fire in 1944, which led to its closure in 1946.
facts.source_title: 6sqft: 52 years ago, Donald Trump's father demolished Coney Island's beloved Steeplechase Park

facts.fact: In 1950 the Luna Park site was razed and rezoned for residential development.
facts.quote: and in 1950, luna was totally razed and rezoned for residential development.

facts.fact: 6sqft says Robert Moses moved the New York Aquarium to the old Dreamland site in 1947 to block another amusement park; other sources date the Coney aquarium cornerstone to 1954 and the opening to 1957 (see conflicts).
facts.quote: in 1947 he moved the new york aquarium to the former home of dreamland to prevent another amusement park from opening.

facts.fact: On April 2, 1953 the New York Times reported that Parks Commissioner Robert Moses proposed rezoning Coney Island for residential use.
facts.quote: on april 2, 1953, the new york times reported that parks commissioner robert moses had put forward a proposal to the city planning commission to rezone coney island for residential use.
facts.source_title: CHPC New York: Coney Island Rezoning (Gems from the Archives)

facts.fact: Low-income housing projects were built on Coney Island beginning in 1954 as the resort declined.
facts.quote: many low-income housing projects were built, beginning in 1954.
facts.source_title: CHPC New York: Coney Island Rezoning

facts.fact: Steeplechase Park, the last of the three big amusement parks, closed in 1964.
facts.quote: steeplechase park, the last of the major parks, closed in 1964.
facts.source_title: CHPC New York: Coney Island Rezoning

facts.fact: Marie Tilyou, majority stockholder, sold all the family's Coney Island property to Fred Trump in February 1965 over her siblings' objections, rejecting local bids from Astroland and Nathan's owners.
facts.quote: sold all the family's coney island property to none other than fred trump (that's right, donald 's father) in february 1965.

facts.fact: Untapped New York says Fred Trump bought Steeplechase in 1964, not 1965 (see conflicts).
facts.quote: fred trump purchased steeplechase park in 1964 with grand hopes to build trump village
facts.source_title: Untapped New York: Fred Trump's demolition of Steeplechase Park

facts.fact: Trump bid for the property through a proxy named Jimmy Onorato, hoping to get a better price by hiding his identity.
facts.quote: fred trump entered the bidding for the property by using a proxy by the name of jimmy onorato.

facts.fact: In 1966, amid efforts to landmark the park, Trump held a demolition party where guests threw bricks at the Steeplechase facade; he then bulldozed it.
facts.quote: people were invited to throw bricks at the facade of steeplechase.

facts.fact: Untapped adds that Trump hired scantily clad models to parade out front and that guests hit the Pavilion of Fun's stained glass; he bulldozed at night, limiting landmarking proceedings. The landmarking motive is the source's account, not proven.
facts.quote: then in the night, he bulldozed the amusement to the ground, thereby limiting any pending proceedings for landmarking.

facts.fact: The bulldozing spared the Parachute Jump, which was designated a landmark in 1977 and is all that remains of Steeplechase.
facts.quote: it was designated an official landmark in 1977

facts.fact: Trump never got the zoning variance to build housing on the site, so he leased it to Norman Kaufman, who ran a makeshift Steeplechase Kiddie Park.
facts.quote: trump never was able to build housing on the site, so he eventually leased it to norman kaufman

facts.fact: The city, which bought the site from Trump in 1969, declined to renew Kaufman's lease in 1981 after other operators complained about his low rent; remnants were torn down two years later.
facts.quote: in 1981, the city (to whom fred trump had sold the site in 1969) wouldn't renew his lease

facts.fact: A minor-league baseball stadium (MCU Park, formerly KeySpan Park) opened on the Steeplechase site in 2001 and is operated by the Mets for the Brooklyn Cyclones.
facts.quote: it wasn't until 2001 that mcu park (formerly keyspan park), a minor league baseball stadium was erected.

facts.fact: Historian Charles Denson wrote that Steeplechase failing to open for the 1965 season created a worldwide impression that all of Coney Island had closed.
facts.quote: when steeplechase closed and failed to open for the 1965 season, the resulting publicity created a worldwide impression that the whole of coney island had closed.
facts.source_title: Untapped New York (quoting Denson, Coney Island Lost and Found)

facts.fact: Denson on why he curated the Trump exhibit: in his view real estate has always been the real business of Coney Island.
facts.quote: to me the real business in coney island has always been real estate and this is part of it.

facts.fact: The Coney Island History Project's exhibit text, as quoted by Untapped, says Trump's tenant relocation tactics at Trump Village harmed poor families who were moved to dilapidated West End bungalows. Attribute to the exhibit; it is an advocacy-side claim.
facts.quote: his racist tenant relocation tactics at the trump village development site destroyed the lives of many poor families
facts.source_title: Untapped New York (quoting Coney Island History Project)

facts.fact: Moses told a 1954-era aquarium audience that when the city took over Coney Island in 1937 it was a honky-tonk waterfront with only about 50 acres of receding, over-crowded beach, and that at high tide there was often no beach at all.
facts.quote: often at high tide there was no beach at all.
facts.source_title: WNYC: Electric Eels Bunking with Tigers: The Itinerant New York Aquarium

facts.fact: In the same recorded speech Moses described the pre-1937 Coney Island as town land given to crooks for a song.
facts.quote: coney was town land owned by the people, given away to crooks for a song

facts.fact: The Coney Island aquarium cornerstone was laid in 1954, when the area was already planned for residential rezoning.
facts.quote: the cornerstone was laid at coney island in 1954.

facts.fact: The Battery Park aquarium closed Oct 1, 1941; WNYC says the aquarium did not re-open until 1957, with a first stage of a $6.5 million plan done by 1956.
facts.quote: the new york aquarium did not re-open until 1957.

facts.fact: At the Coney opening a black-footed penguin named Annie cut the ribbon by biting a wrapped smelt, and children poured in.
facts.quote: annie, a black footed penguin, served as the ribbon cutter by biting at a wrapped smelt fish.

facts.fact: Moses in 1941 called the Battery aquarium an ugly wart on the axis to the Statue of Liberty; he wanted it gone for the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, which is why a new home was needed.
facts.quote: the aquarium is an ugly wart on the main axis leading straight to the statue of liberty

facts.fact: Postwar urban renewal put high-rise housing where amusements had been, including the Coney Island Houses (1956) and the Warbasse Houses (1966).
facts.quote: including the warbasse houses (1966) and the coney island houses (1956)

facts.fact: A 1974 CHPC report was written in response to a court order to desegregate Mark Twain Junior High, and argued the whole neighborhood had to be made more attractive.
facts.quote: a court order demanding the desegregation of coney islands mark twain junior high school
facts.source_title: CHPC New York: Coney Island Rezoning

facts.fact: 6sqft says crime rose in the 1960s and hurt attendance at the surviving parks.
facts.quote: by the '60s, coney island saw a rise in crime, affecting attendance at steeplechase and the surrounding parks.

facts.fact: Astroland opened in 1962 as a 3.1-acre space-age park at 1000 Surf Avenue (West 10th Street) beside the boardwalk.
facts.quote: astroland was a 3.1-acre (1.3 ha) amusement park in coney island, brooklyn, new york city that opened in 1962.

facts.fact: Astroland's theme was inspired by astronaut John Glenn's orbit; early rides simulated trips to the moon for 50 cents.
facts.quote: skyrocketed coney into an exciting new era inspired by astronaut john glenn's historic trek as the first american in orbit
facts.source_title: Brooklyn Paper: Astroland founder Jerry Albert dies at 74

facts.fact: Early Astroland rides included the Cape Canaveral Satellite Jet, a Mercury capsule skyride, and the Tower to the Stars (AstroTower).
facts.quote: the mercury capsule skyride carrying patrons in bubble cars across the park to the boardwalk

facts.fact: In mid-1975 the Albert family's Astroland took over operating the Cyclone, which sat on Parks Department land; the city had been about to demolish it.
facts.quote: the alberts also rushed to coney's rescue in the mid-1970s, when the city decided to demolish the world-famous cyclone roller coaster.

facts.fact: An early-morning fire on July 12, 1975 wiped out much of Astroland, but the park rebuilt.
facts.quote: on july 12, 1975, an early-morning fire wiped out much of the park, but they were able to rebuild.

facts.fact: The Cyclone was landmarked in 1988.
facts.quote: the beloved cyclone, which was landmarked in 1988

facts.fact: Dick Zigun recalled Jerry Albert bragging that Astroland had no graffiti, no burned-out bulb and no cracked sidewalk.
facts.quote: jerry used to brag that astroland was the place where there wasn't a bit of graffiti, not one light bulb burned out, and not one crack in the sidewalks

facts.fact: Lou Powsner said Astroland turned Coney from a depression-era nickel-and-dime resort into a world-class amusement mecca after Steeplechase closed in 1964.
facts.quote: it gave a necessary injection into the dormant era of amusements

facts.fact: The Albert family sold Astroland to Thor Equities on Nov 28, 2006 for $30 million; Thor announced a $1.5 billion year-round resort that never came to fruition.
facts.quote: on november 28, 2006, astroland was sold by the albert family for us$30 million to thor equities

facts.fact: Astroland closed for good on September 7, 2008 after talks between the Alberts and Thor failed.
facts.quote: astroland closed on september 7, 2008.

facts.fact: Luna Park, a new park named after the original, opened May 29, 2010 on the former Astroland site.
facts.quote: opened for the 2010 season on may 29, 2010, at the former site of astroland.

facts.fact: On July 2-4, 2013 Luna Park was evacuated when the AstroTower swayed; the top was cut down overnight and the park reopened at 3 p.m. July 4; by July 6 only a four-foot stump remained.
facts.quote: an initial portion of the astrotower was taken down beginning the night of july 3, 2013.

facts.fact: The Astroland rocket now sits as a historical monument inside Deno's Wonder Wheel Park, with signs by the Coney Island History Project.
facts.quote: installed as a historical monument inside neighboring deno's wonder wheel park

facts.fact: The City Council approved the controversial Coney Island amusement-district rezoning on July 29, 2009.
facts.quote: the new york city council approved the controversial rezoning of the coney island amusement district back on july 29.

facts.fact: The plan created a 27-acre amusement district between Surf Avenue and the boardwalk, but only 12 acres were reserved for outdoor rides; the rest could be indoor amusements and up to four hotels.
facts.quote: only 12 of those acres would be reserved for outdoor rollercoasters

facts.fact: The Save Coney Island coalition sued the city on Nov 25, 2009, saying the rezoning favored developer Thor Equities.
facts.quote: filed the suit at new york state supreme court in manhattan on november 25 on behalf of the save coney island coalition.

facts.fact: After the city deal, Thor and Joe Sitt kept about four acres in Coney Island; amusements had shrunk to inflatable rides while the dispute dragged on.
facts.quote: thor equities and its principal joe sitt still retains about four acres of land in coney island

facts.fact: Sea Gate, the gated community at Coney's western tip, has about 8,000 residents with private beaches and views of the Verrazzano Bridge.
facts.quote: today, sea gate is home to about 8,000 residents who enjoy private beaches and expansive views of the verrazano bridge

facts.fact: Hurricane Sandy's surge eroded the shore so badly that Coney Island Beach lost 600,000 cubic yards of sand.
facts.quote: coney island beach lost 600,000 cubic yards of sand.

facts.fact: In 2013 the Army Corps placed about 580,000 cubic yards of sand on Coney Island Beach to restore its authorized design, funded by the 2013 Sandy relief law.
facts.quote: in 2013, approximately 580,000 cubic yards of sand

facts.fact: The Corps says the raised beach avoided an estimated $494 million in damage to houses and structures during Sandy.
facts.quote: avoided an estimated $494 million in damages

facts.fact: Sandy's surge pushed sand and water up and over the boardwalk, but the elevated beach limited damage behind it.
facts.quote: hurricane sandy's surge pushed sand and water up and over

facts.fact: The magazine says Coney Island Beach turned 100 years old in 2023.
facts.quote: this year, coney island beach turns 100-years-old

facts.fact: Sea Gate stone project (Army Corps): a $25.2 million contract for four stone T-groins, a spur on the West 37th Street groin, and reinforcement of the Norton Point dike; about 100,000 tons of stone.
facts.quote: crews working under a $25.2 million contract are first carrying out the stonework portions of the project
facts.source_title: Dredging Today: Sea Gate project makes progress

facts.fact: The Sea Gate project's main purpose is to protect the West 37th Street terminal groin from flanking and slow erosion of fill on Coney Island's Atlantic side west to Norton Point.
facts.quote: reduce rapid erosion of fill on the atlantic coast of coney island/sea gate that occurs from that groin westward to norton point
facts.source_title: Dredging Today: Sea Gate project makes progress

facts.fact: Planned sand for Sea Gate was about 125,000 cubic yards, from the Gravesend Bay side of Sea Gate and dredging of the Rockaway Inlet channel; the project is 100 percent federally funded under the 2013 Sandy relief act.
facts.quote: the project also includes the placement of roughly 125,000 cubic yards of sand
facts.source_title: Dredging Today: Sea Gate project makes progress

facts.fact: The 2023 magazine says in 2016 the Corps built four stone groins at Sea Gate and placed 75,000 cubic yards of dredged sand around them.
facts.quote: placing 75,000 cubic yards of dredged sand

facts.fact: After Sandy, Coney Island bounced back and the parks reopened the following year, so the Mermaid Parade and Nathan's contest went on.
facts.quote: coney island bounced back

facts.fact: Activist Craig Hammerman says Sandy's worst flooding in Coney Island came from the creek overflowing, not the ocean.
facts.quote: it was [the] creek flooding over that really hit the community the hardest during sandy, it wasn't the ocean as much
facts.source_title: City Limits: The quest to clean up Coney Island Creek, part 3

facts.fact: The Army Corps released its draft NY-NJ Harbor and Tributaries (HATS) plan on Sept 26, 2022; the Coney Island History Project called the $52 billion plan a shocker for Coney Island.
facts.quote: the proposed $52 billion plan for new york and parts of new jersey
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: What the Army Corps' NY coastal resiliency plan means for Coney Island

facts.fact: On the ocean side the plan would raise the boardwalk five feet with a wide concrete walkway acting as a surge barrier.
facts.quote: the boardwalk would be raised five feet by adding what appears to be a wide concrete walkway
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: Comments needed for Coney Island flood control plan

facts.fact: Denson says the concrete barrier would block ocean views for boardwalk businesses and take up about a third of the boardwalk.
facts.quote: the concrete barrier would block ocean views for boardwalk businesses as well as taking up about a third of the boardwalk
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: Comments needed

facts.fact: On the creek side the plan calls for a mechanical tide gate from Neptune Avenue to Calvert Vaux Park, tied to sea walls and flood walls along Kaiser Park and Coney Island Creek Park, curving around Sea Gate to the boardwalk at West 37th Street.
facts.quote: a mechanical tide gate in coney island creek stretching from neptune avenue to calvert vaux park
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: Comments needed

facts.fact: The 2022 post says the plan would be finalized in two years and construction would begin in 2030; the Corps only submits the plan to Congress, which appropriates funds. Status after 2023 is unverified.
facts.quote: the plan will be finalized in two years, and construction begins in 2030.
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: What the plan means

facts.fact: The Corps labeled its renderings initial concepts that may change; comment deadline was extended from Jan 6, 2023 to March 31, 2023.
facts.quote: a march 31, 2023 deadline to submit public comments about the plan is fast approaching.
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: Comments needed

facts.fact: At Neptune Avenue and West 21st Street, Sandy erosion went unrepaired for 10 years, and in a king tide the creek rises higher than the street.
facts.quote: during a king tide the water level in the creek is higher than the street.
facts.source_title: Coney Island History Project: Comments needed

facts.fact: On March 12, 2012 the Public Design Commission voted 6-0 to let Parks replace the wooden boardwalk between Coney Island Avenue and Brighton 15th Street with concrete and recycled plastic lumber.
facts.quote: the commission's 6-0 vote gives the parks department permission to tear out the wooden boardwalk between coney island avenue and brighton 15th street
facts.source_title: Brooklyn Paper: City: concrete, plastic to replace boardwalk's wood

facts.fact: The 2012 design: a 12-foot-wide concrete lane for emergency vehicles with 19-foot plastic-lumber paths on each side.
facts.quote: a 19-foot pathway built out of recycled plastic boards will be put on either side of the concrete path
facts.source_title: Brooklyn Paper: concrete, plastic to replace boardwalk's wood

facts.fact: The boardwalk is a 2.7-mile span that opened in 1923; Parks planned a $30 million renovation.
facts.quote: 2.7-mile span, which opened in 1923

facts.fact: Parks said concrete cost $90 per square foot, roughly $40 cheaper than real wood; a later article gave $114 per square foot for concrete topped with plastic lumber (see conflicts).
facts.quote: at $90 per square foot - roughly $40 per square foot cheaper than real wood

facts.fact: Opponents were loud: more than 40 people testified against the plan in a four-hour hearing, and Rob Burstein called it a sad day for Coney Island.
facts.quote: more than 40 people testified against the city's plan during a raucous four-hour hearing.

facts.fact: Parks designer Alex Hart said the city would prefer wood but found nothing that works; black locust was considered and rejected on cost.
facts.quote: we would greatly prefer to use wood

facts.fact: In 2010 Parks first proposed replacing the whole boardwalk with concrete and plastic lumber except a four-block historic stretch between West 15th and West 10th Streets.
facts.quote: except for a four-block section in the historic amusement district between w. 15th and w. 10th streets

facts.fact: In May 2011 Parks cut the concrete lane from 16 to 12 feet; critics worried concrete would scorch feet, crack and get slippery, while Parks said tests showed concrete was more durable and not slippery.
facts.quote: the agency concluded that concrete was more durable than faux wood and didn't get slippery.
facts.source_title: Brooklyn Paper: new faux boardwalk will have less cement

facts.fact: In 2011 the city said concrete cost $90 per square foot versus $114 for a concrete slab topped with recycled plastic lumber.
facts.quote: concrete costs $90 per square-foot, compared to $114 per square foot for a concrete slab topped with recycled plastic lumber
